canonical_topic: Exception to no-early-exercise: dividends accrue to the stock owner, not the option owner
definition: Owning the underlying asset can carry a benefit the option owner never receives — for example, a stock dividend. Since a dividend payment reduces the stock price (and thus a call option's value) but only the stock owner collects the offsetting cash, a call holder may rationally exercise early to capture a large dividend, giving up the option's remaining extrinsic value in exchange for it.
core_idea: Early exercise can make sense specifically when the underlying delivers a benefit the option contract itself does not pass through, and that benefit is large enough to outweigh the extrinsic value being forfeited.
key_points: A stock dividend lowers the stock price and thus reduces a call option's value.
The stock owner is compensated for that price drop by receiving the dividend cash; the call option owner is not.
If the dividend is large enough, it can be worthwhile for a call holder to exercise early and give up the extrinsic value in order to capture the dividend as a stockholder.
relationships: Named as the exception to the general no-early-exercise rule
trading_implications: This exception is specific to options on assets (like dividend-paying stocks) where holding the underlying itself confers a benefit not passed through the option contract.
